title: Pass-through, transform, mediation
summary: Recognise the three shapes of an API, and know when an integration layer is the wrong answer.

steps.title: Three shapes
body: Every API you publish falls into one of three shapes:
- **Pass-through**: the gateway calls the backend directly. The backend already speaks a clean contract
for consumers; the gateway only adds security, subscriptions and rate limits. No integration code.
- **Transform**: an integration sits between them and **reshapes**: validates input, renames fields, hides
internal fields, maps backend errors to your error contract.
- **Mediation**: the integration does more than reshape. It adds a backend credential consumers must never see,
translates in both directions, bridges protocols (REST in, SOAP or a database out), or **orchestrates**
several backend calls into one answer.
```text
pass-through:  gateway ───────────────► backend
transform:     gateway ──► integration ──► backend      (reshape, hide, map errors)
mediation:     gateway ──► integration ──► backend A + backend B + secret key

items: The shipping-rates service already returns a clean, documented JSON contract
The catalogue returns `internalCost`, which consumers must never see
Rename `sku_code` to `isbn` and map a backend 404 to our error body
The carrier API needs Acme's own API key on every call
Consumers send JSON; the billing system only speaks SOAP
One `GET /orders/{id}` answer combines the order service and the carrier's tracking API

steps.title: When NOT to add an integration layer
body: An integration layer costs latency, code, a container to run, and an on-call rotation. Skip it when:
- **The API is a pass-through.** Publish it on the gateway. A Camel route that forwards bytes unchanged adds
nothing but a hop.
- **The logic is business logic.** Pricing, eligibility and stock rules belong in the service that owns the
data. An integration that "just adds one rule" becomes the hidden owner of the business.
- **You would build one giant project.** One project holding every API means every change redeploys every API.
Split by business domain.
And never publish a **generic "do anything" endpoint** (run any query the caller writes, call any internal URL the caller names,
proxy any URL). Onboarding an existing API means *choosing what to expose*, not exposing everything it can do:
replace it with specific operations.

steps.prompt: The shipping-rates service has a clean OpenAPI contract, no secrets to add and nothing to hide. Consumers need it behind a token and a rate limit. What do you build?
options: Publish it on the gateway as a pass-through, with no integration layer
A Camel route that forwards the request unchanged
A new microservice that wraps it
Nothing: let consumers call it directly
steps.explain: The gateway alone gives you tokens, subscriptions and limits. A forwarding route would only add latency and something to maintain. Calling it directly would skip the gateway's protection.

steps.prompt: An existing reporting API has `POST /execute` that runs whatever SQL text the caller sends. A partner wants report data. What do you do?
options: Never publish it as is: design specific operations (for example `GET /reports/sales?month=`) in an integration that runs only the queries you chose
Publish it behind the gateway, since the gateway checks tokens
Publish it, but rate-limit it to 10 calls a minute
Publish it and document which queries partners may send
steps.explain: A token proves who the caller is; it does not limit *what* a generic endpoint lets them do. Every table in the database becomes part of your public API.

steps.prompt: Match each smell to the better design.
pairs: Route that forwards requests byte for byte
Publish the backend as a pass-through on the gateway
Discount rules inside an integration route
Move the rule into the service that owns prices
One integration project with every API in it
Endpoint that runs any query the caller sends
Backend password typed into the consumer's app
Integration adds the backend credential from configuration

code: string Shape(bool hidesFields, bool addsSecret, bool combinesCalls)
steps.explain: Check the strongest need first. An API that both hides fields and adds a secret is mediation: it needs everything a transform does, and more.

steps.title: Onboarding decisions
prompt: record ApiFacts(bool GenericExecute, bool NeedsBackendSecret, bool CallsSeveralBackends,
bool ProtocolChange, bool HidesFields, bool RenamesFields, bool NeedsValidation);
Write `string Onboard(ApiFacts f)` returning, in this order of precedence:
2. `"mediation"` if it needs a backend secret, calls several backends, or changes protocol;
3. `"transform"` if it hides fields, renames fields or needs validation;
hints: Check the conditions in exactly the order listed and `return` as soon as one matches.
template: Dojo.Eq("clean contract -> pass-through", "pass-through", Onboard(new ApiFacts(false, false, false, false, false, false, false)));
Dojo.Eq("hides internalCost -> transform", "transform", Onboard(new ApiFacts(false, false, false, false, true, false, false)));
Dojo.Eq("needs validation only -> transform", "transform", Onboard(new ApiFacts(false, false, false, false, false, false, true)));
Dojo.Eq("SOAP backend -> mediation", "mediation", Onboard(new ApiFacts(false, false, false, true, false, false, false)));
Dojo.Eq("secret + renames -> mediation", "mediation", Onboard(new ApiFacts(false, true, false, false, false, true, false)));
Dojo.Eq("two backends -> mediation", "mediation", Onboard(new ApiFacts(false, false, true, false, false, false, false)));
Dojo.Eq("generic execute -> redesign, whatever else is true", "redesign", Onboard(new ApiFacts(true, true, true, true, true, true, true)));
record ApiFacts(bool GenericExecute, bool NeedsBackendSecret, bool CallsSeveralBackends, bool ProtocolChange, bool HidesFields, bool RenamesFields, bool NeedsValidation);
